newsitem.title: UK: UK's FTSE to stagnate over next two years - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK's FTSE to stagnate over next two years - survey.

text.p: British stocks will end this year little changed from current levels, stifled by political uncertainty and expectations of higher interest rates, according to analysts in a Reuters poll of stock index forecasts published on Wednesday.
The median prediction from 13 London-based stock market analysts put the FTSE-100 index at 4,400 by the end of 1997, just off its all-time closing high of 4,444.3 reached on March 11 this year.
The FTSE closed at 4,397.7 on March 13, the last day of the poll which began on March 10. It closed down 16.5 on Tuesday at 4,356.8.
Analysts were also cautious on the outlook for 1998. An average of eight forecasts is for the market to rise by just five percent from current levels, to 4,625 by the end of 1998.
Strategists said the market is likely to struggle to make headway under the Labour government which is the odds-on result of the general election being held on May 1.
"The FTSE is going down because the Conservatives are going to lose the election. The equity market will react badly," said Steve Wright, equity strategist at BZW, whose year-end target is 4,300.

David Aserkoff, strategist at CS First Boston, said the political risk was two-fold -- what policies a likely Labour government would enact, and also the fact that the Labour party would enter with virtually zero experience in government.
"They are used to being a party in opposition and not a party of government," Aserkoff said. His year-end forecast for the FTSE 100 is 4,475.
Kevin Gardiner, Morgan Stanley's UK economist, agreed there was a policy risk associated with a Labour victory.

"There is ... the possibility of a change in taxation with a Labour government. In particular I'd be looking at the possibility of a change in dividend taxation and possibly even a change in corporate taxation," he said.
A likely hike in interest rates could also keep a lid on stock market growth.
"Interest rates are going to go up sharply," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse Tilney, who expects the FTSE 100 to end 1997 at 4,000.
"There may be a lull in domestic demand at the moment, but the second half of this year will be much more active and the government will have to react with higher interest rates," Jeffrey said.
A monetary tightening normally has a negative impact on the market as it means firms must pay more for the money they borrow and slows the economy, dampening profit growth.
Higher interest rates also raise the relative appeal for investors of ordinary bank and building society deposits.
Meantime sterling's stubbornly high level could hamper profit growth and has already prompted a flurry of FTSE-100 companies to warn investors of depressed growth in 1997.
While the outlook for 1998 is less gloomy, the market is unlikely to take off.
"I think the economy is fairly firm. As a result interest rates will continue to rise," said Gardiner.

"The flip side of a strong economy is that (company) earnings could continue to do quite well, but I think as we go through 1998, increasingly the possibility of a cyclical downturn in earnings growth is going to increase as the market begins to discount very sharp slowdowns in the economy maybe in 1999."
